Sam Bankman-Fried co-founded Alameda Research in 2017 and FTX in 2019 as a complement to it. Within two years of FTX's founding, over 80 investors provided approximately $2 billion in capital. In January 2022, FTX raised $400 million in a Series C round, boosting its valuation to $32 billion. In early November 2022, CoinDesk published Alameda's balance sheet showing $14.6 billion in assets and $8 billion in liabilities as of June 30, 2022. Alameda's largest asset was $3.66 billion of 'unlocked FTT' and $2.16 billion of 'FTT collateral'. Alameda owned $5.82 billion in FTT tokens, which was 193% higher than the total FTT market cap of about $3 billion. In early November 2022, Binance pulled out its remaining $2.1 billion equivalent of cash in BUSD and FTT, triggering a bank run on FTX. FTX and Alameda filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in the U.S. in mid-November 2022. Sam Bankman-Fried resigned as CEO and John J. Ray III was appointed the new CEO. SBF maintained his innocence, stating he did not try to commit fraud and was shocked by what happened. SBF was arrested in the Bahamas in December 2022, extradited to the U.S., and released on $250 million bail; his house arrest in Palo Alto was revoked in August following a diary leak accusation. During testimony, John J. Ray III stated that House Financial Services had virtually no internal controls, no separateness, and did not trust a single piece of paper; U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called the crimes the biggest financial fraud in American history. Gary Wang and Caroline Ellison pleaded guilty in December 2022 to federal charges and face civil penalties from the SEC and CFTC, planning to cooperate as witnesses. SBF pleaded not guilty in January to wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering, and conspiracy to misuse customer funds, facing up to 115 years in jail if convicted. The FTX collapse was the first of many, with BlockFi filing for Chapter 11 in November 2022 and Genesis Global Trading filing for Chapter 11 in January.

* [SBF's $5B offer to Trump to cancel presidential bid and FTX collapse](sbf-s-5b-offer-to-trump-to-cancel-presidential-bid-and-ftx.md) - SBF offered $5 billion to Donald Trump to cancel his 2024 re-run; he was accused of orchestrating FTX's collapse, raised $2B from major VCs, and faced criticism for his management style and financial dealings.

    before first witnesses take the stand

The trial against former FTX CEO Sam Bankman-Fried began with opening statements on the second day, following jury selection on Wednesday morning. The prosecution, led by Thane Rehn, alleged that SBF stole billions from thousands of victims and lied to the world. They detailed a scheme involving Alameda Research and Caroline Ellison to gain secret access to customer funds, with actions including directing employees to conceal money flows and forging financial documents. The prosecution characterized SBF as a 'man' who built a thriving exchange, traveled internationally, and financed risky bets, claiming all his public appearances were built on lies.

In contrast, defense attorney Mark Cohen presented SBF as a well-meaning startup founder who acted in 'good faith,' arguing he did not defraud anyone. Cohen noted SBF's appearance, which showed more prominent cheekbones after spending seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison, and aimed to present him as anything but the prosecution's 'cartoon of a villain.' SBF himself described Alameda as a successful hedge fund and FTX as an innovative company, not a Ponzi scheme. He argued Alameda acted legally as a customer, payment processor, and market maker, using the analogy that 'working at a startup is like building a plane as you're flying it.' SBF blamed Ellison for not adequately protecting the hedge fund from market risks and claimed he offered to give up personal wealth when the crisis approached, concluding he built two billion-dollar businesses without stealing money.

Witness testimony began with Marc-Antoine Julliard, a Paris-born cocoa trader living in London who invested in FTX in 2021. Julliard testified that he attempted to withdraw almost $100,000 on November 8, 2021, but never succeeded. Adam Yedidia, an MIT graduate and close friend of SBF, testified that he had legal immunity and persuaded SBF to join him as a trader at Alameda and developer at FTX after SBF left Jane Street, citing concern that he had unwittingly written code contributing to a crime. The court adjourned at 4:30 p.m., with Yedidia scheduled to continue testimony on Thursday, followed by Matt Huang and Gary Wang.

* [SBF's trial and the rise and fall of FTX](sbf-s-trial-and-the-rise-and-fall-of-ftx.md) - This note covers the start of SBF's fraud trial, the founding of FTX and Alameda, the 2022 collapse triggered by Binance's withdrawal, the subsequent bankruptcy, SBF's arrest and extradition, and the guilty pleas of other executives.

FTX and Alameda filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in the U.S. in mid-November 2022. Sam Bankman-Fried resigned as CEO and John J. Ray III was appointed the new CEO. SBF maintained his innocence, stating he did not try to commit fraud and was shocked by what happened. SBF was arrested in the Bahamas in December 2022, extradited to the U.S., and released on $250 million bail; his house arrest in Palo Alto was revoked in August following a diary leak accusation. During testimony, John J. Ray III stated that House Financial Services had virtually no internal controls, no separateness, and did not trust a single piece of paper; U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called the crimes the biggest financial fraud in American history. Gary Wang and Caroline Ellison pleaded guilty in December 2022 to federal charges and face civil penalties from the SEC and CFTC, planning to cooperate as witnesses. SBF pleaded not guilty in January to wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering, and conspiracy to misuse customer funds, facing up to 115 years in jail if convicted. The FTX collapse was the first of many, with BlockFi filing for Chapter 11 in November 2022 and Genesis Global Trading filing for Chapter 11 in January.

Title: Sam Bankman-Fried Trial Opening Statements and Witness Testimony
Summary: Details the prosecution and defense opening statements in the SBF trial, including key allegations, the defense's characterization of SBF, and the testimony of early witnesses like Marc-Antoine Julliard and Adam Yedidia.

The trial against former FTX CEO Sam Bankman-Fried began with opening statements on the second day, following jury selection on Wednesday morning. The prosecution, led by Thane Rehn, alleged that SBF stole billions from thousands of victims and lied to the world. They detailed a scheme involving Alameda Research and Caroline Ellison to gain secret access to customer funds, with actions including directing employees to conceal money flows and forging financial documents. The prosecution characterized SBF as a 'man' who built a thriving exchange, traveled internationally, and financed risky bets, claiming all his public appearances were built on lies.

In contrast, defense attorney Mark Cohen presented SBF as a well-meaning startup founder who acted in 'good faith,' arguing he did not defraud anyone. Cohen noted SBF's appearance, which showed more prominent cheekbones after spending seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison, and aimed to present him as anything but the prosecution's 'cartoon of a villain.' SBF himself described Alameda as a successful hedge fund and FTX as an innovative company, not a Ponzi scheme. He argued Alameda acted legally as a customer, payment processor, and market maker, using the analogy that 'working at a startup is like building a plane as you're flying it.' SBF blamed Ellison for not adequately protecting the hedge fund from market risks and claimed he offered to give up personal wealth when the crisis approached, concluding he built two billion-dollar businesses without stealing money.

Witness testimony began with Marc-Antoine Julliard, a Paris-born cocoa trader living in London who invested in FTX in 2021. Julliard testified that he attempted to withdraw almost $100,000 on November 8, 2021, but never succeeded. Adam Yedidia, an MIT graduate and close friend of SBF, testified that he had legal immunity and persuaded SBF to join him as a trader at Alameda and developer at FTX after SBF left Jane Street, citing concern that he had unwittingly written code contributing to a crime. The court adjourned at 4:30 p.m., with Yedidia scheduled to continue testimony on Thursday, followed by Matt Huang and Gary Wang.
